own_scenes.desc: Término que Hannett aplicó a Joy Division y luego insulto para los epígonos, hasta que en 1982 los fans lo adoptan como estandarte frente a la excesiva luminosidad del new pop: glamour sepulcral, retorno de lo reprimido, emociones atemporales. Bauhaus («Bela Lugosi's Dead», 1979, el comienzo propiamente dicho; Peter Murphy, sex symbol heredero de Adam Ant y Bowie), The Birthday Party (el gótico americano de Nick Cave: «Release the Bats», Junkyard), Killing Joke («música de tensión», del funk de PiL a Black Sabbath, con un aura inquietante), The Cure (gótico light: Seventeen Seconds, Faith, Pornography). El club The Batcave (1982), el «positive punk», Southern Death Cult, Theatre of Hate, The Sisters of Mercy («¡Nosotros sí somos una banda de rock!»), el death rock de Los Ángeles y Kukl con Björk. Su deriva: coqueteos totalitarios y la conversión en versión postpunk del heavy metal (The Cult).

refs.q: La genealogía de la palabra "gótico" abarca iglesias medievales
refs.para: EL REGRESO DEL ROC K CON EL GÓTICO Y LA N U EVA PSICODE LIA La genealogía de la palabra "gótico" abarca iglesias medievales, una tendencia literaria y artística centrada en la muerte y lo sobrenatural, y al pueblo originario de los godos, bárbaros germánicos que invadieron el Imperio Romano durante su época de mayor decadencia. En el mundo del postpunk, "gótico"
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Oscuridad y juventud gloriosa: el regreso del rock con el gótico y la nueva psicodelia

refs.q: El epicentro de la escena gótica en un principio fue The Batcave
refs.para: El epicentro de la escena gótica en un principio fue The Batcave, un club nocturno de SoHo donde el funk estaba "terminantemente prohibido" y cuyas puertas se abrieron en julio de 1982, como una alternativa al new romanticism y a la música dance negra de las discotecas londinenses. Fundado por la banda camp Specimen, el local estaba decorado con adornos de cuero, tachas y afiches de películas de monstruos de la década del treinta. El club pronto alcanzó un éxito considerable y emprendió giras por diversas provincias, inspiró imitadores y patrocinó eventos en todo el Reino Unido, hasta llegar a organizar una fiesta en Danceteria, en Nueva York.
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Oscuridad y juventud gloriosa: el regreso del rock con el gótico y la nueva psicodelia

refs.q: Lo que unificaba todos esos rasgos diversos era una visión romántica del pasado
refs.para: Lo que unificaba todos esos rasgos diversos era una visión romántica del pasado. El movimiento gótico original de la literatura del siglo XVIII y principios del XIX fue antimodernista, y significó el retorno de lo reprimido, de todas las supersticiones medievales y los deseos primordiales supuestamente desterrados por la Revolución Industrial durante la Ilustración. La nueva corriente gótica también se basaba en la idea de que las emociones más profundas se remontan miles de años en el pasado: se trataba de las experiencias fundamentales y eternas del amor, la muerte, la desesperación, la admiración y el temor.
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Oscuridad y juventud gloriosa: el regreso del rock con el gótico y la nueva psicodelia

refs.q: el tema que Bauhaus compuso acerca del vampirismo, "Bela Lugosi's Dead"
refs.para: …otros dos EP geniales poco después, The Bad Seed y Mutiny. Algunas de las mejores canciones de esos discos son "Deep in che Woods", con inquietantes árboles que hablan; "Swampland", un relato sureño mitad Faulkner y mitad Deliverance; y "Mutiny in Heaven", una descripción blasfema del cielo, donde abundan la corrupción, las ruinas, la basura y las ratas, acompañada de instrumentos sorprendentemente vívidos, con un sonido retorcido y pútrido. En términos de influencia en la escena gótica, sin embargo, la canción más importante del grupo fue "Release che Bacs", editada en 1981. El single -que describía, rayando el camp, una re!ación sexual vampírica- llegó a la cima de los rankings independientes, y se lo publicitó con avisos que rezaban: "Dirciness is next to antigocUiness" . 1 No obstante, el tema que Bauhaus compuso acerca del vampirismo, "Bela Lugosi's Dead", editado en 1979, es la canción que suele considerarse el comienzo del gótico propiamente dicho. El viscoso look del cancanee, Pecer Murphy -altísimo, pálido, de labios morados y pómulos perfectos-, lo convirtió en un ícono del movimiento y un enigma erótico. Sin embargo, lo que salía de esos sensuales labios era impactante y ridículo, una letanía exagerada de sexo, muerte, religión y blasfemia con una voz que imitaba la de Bowie a la

refs.q: Las tendencias nazis latentes en el movimiento gótico eran un motivo de preocupación
refs.para: Las tendencias nazis latentes en el movimiento gótico eran un motivo de preocupación. La costumbre de provocar recurriendo a imágenes fascistas se puede rastrear hasta Joy Division y Siouxsie (quien, en sus comienws, portaba una esvástica y cantaba el imperdonable verso "Hay demasiados judíos para mi gusto"). The March Violets tomaron su nombre del término que usaban los alemanes para referirse a los oportunistas que se unieron al partido nazi en 1934, después de que Hitler se declarara Führer. La música de Kirk Brandon motivó comparaciones con el nazismo desde los inicios de su carrera con Theatre of Hate. Para peor, Brandon tenía las facciones clásicas del arquetipo ario y cantaba con un estilo operístico; editó los primeros discos de su banda a través del sello SS; y, junto con los otros integrantes, solía pasar "La cabalgata de las valquirias" de Wagner antes de cada recital. Sus temas más emblemáticos y alegóricos, como "Do You Believe in the Westworld?", aspiraban a la épica política, pero sus letras confusas dejaban entrever una ideología muy cuestionable. Lo que no podía negarse era el deseo del cantante de proyectarse como un líder mesiánico. "No somos una banda -declaró- somos un movimiento".

similar_scenes.name: Dark punk y rock gótico
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: El punk británico estuvo flanqueado desde el principio por un movimiento «gótico» que canalizaba su violencia hacia atmósferas de terror y rituales esotéricos: Stranglers, Siouxsie, X-Ray Spex. Lo más interesante evita el tono de película de terror: The Cure introducen la angustia existencial de Camus y Sartre (Pornography, Disintegration); Joy Division mezclan Doors, Kraftwerk y Black Sabbath y su final anuncia el synth-pop; Bauhaus, Killing Joke, Psychedelic Furs, los irlandeses Virgin Prunes y la cima del género, Public Image Ltd de Johnny Lydon, que convierte el punk en música de cámara con dub y ecos étnicos (Second Edition, Flowers Of Romance). Después, el gótico bailable de Sisters Of Mercy, Alien Sex Fiend, Cult, Mission e In The Nursery.

similar_scenes.name: Rock gótico de los noventa
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: El gótico, más una actitud que un sonido, se refina en los noventa con mejores estudios y teclados electrónicos, y su liderazgo pasa de Gran Bretaña a EE UU. En Alemania, Das Ich (Staub); en Suecia, la escuela «constructivista» de ambient-gótico-industrial (Brighter Death Now, Raison D'Etre, Arcana, Deutsch Nepal), más cerca de la música clásica que del rock. En EE UU, el sello Projekt: Lycia, Black Tape For A Blue Girl, Love Spirals Downwards, Faith And The Muse, Rasputina; en Europa del Este, los herederos de Laibach; en Australia, Shinjuku Thief.

podcast.title: Appearance (1978-1979)
podcast.body: Goth music first emerged around 1978-1979, primarily from the UK. It was a crucial precursor for the development of Dreampop.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Generation (1979-1985)
podcast.body: The first distinct wave of Goth bands was active from 1979 until approximately the end of 1985, with Britain leading this initial development. "The first generation of Goth bands existed from 1979 through to about the end of 1985."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Batcave as Turning Point (1982-1983)
podcast.body: The period between the summer of 1982 and the end of 1983, particularly with the opening of The Batcave club, marked a significant turning point, providing a central hub for the Goth subculture to take root and flourish. "The big turning point for Goth came between the summer of 1982 and the end of 1983..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstream Break in Early 1983
podcast.body: Goth found its way into the mainstream in early 1983, largely due to the British music media and public becoming bored with "bouncy, lightweight technopop," leading to Goths becoming "new darlings" on the indie charts. "Goth's big break into the mainstream came in early 1983."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: End of First Wave (Late 1985)
podcast.body: By the end of 1985, the first wave of Goth and "Goth Mania" began to recede, yet the music and subculture demonstrated a lasting resilience, proving "just as undead as some of their subjects of fascination." "By the end of 1985 the first wave of Goth and Goth Mania was coming to an end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 80s Alt-Rock Radio Inclusion
podcast.body: Goth music was among the diverse genres featured on alt-rock radio playlists in the 1980s, demonstrating the broad range of music played before the rise of grunge.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Basic Enduring Sound
podcast.body: Goth music is listed as one of the basic and enduring sounds that will never go away, but is continuously challenged by new genres. "The basic sounds are still with us. Rock, alternative, indie, Goth, industrial, metal, synth-based music, ska, reggae, and so on. They're never going to go away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Bowie as a Looming Presence
podcast.body: For fans of Goth music, David Bowie loomed as a significant presence, influencing bands like Depeche Mode, The Cure, Suede, and New Order. "If you were a fan of Goth, Bowie loomed as a presence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Pervasive Presence
podcast.body: David Bowie loomed as a significant presence for anyone involved in goth music, with his influence clearly visible in bands like Depeche Mode, The Cure, and New Order. His genre-bending work and theatricality were foundational to the genre's development. "If you were into any kind of goth, Bowie loomed as a presence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Role in "The Hunger" and Goth Appeal
podcast.body: David Bowie's portrayal of a vampire in the 1983 film "The Hunger" endeared him to Goth fans, further solidifying his connection and influence within that subculture. "He played a vampire in the hunger, something that endeared him to Goth fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Box Set History
podcast.body: A box set specifically detailing the history of Goth music is mentioned, indicating how comprehensive compilations can be dedicated to exploring specific genres. "Here's one that details the history of Goth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Goth Movement - Defining Elements
podcast.body: The British Goth movement, pioneered by bands like Bauhaus, was characterized by its glamour, energy, art school sensibilities, and an overriding attitude of "doom and gloom." This particular sound, look, and attitude became highly infectious and spread globally. "The glamour, the energy, the art school sensibilities, and the attitude of doom and gloom proved to be infectious."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Bauhaus

podcast.title: British Goth Movement Origins
podcast.body: The British Goth movement found its pace with Bauhaus's debut album "In A Flat Field" in 1980. Bauhaus is considered one of the founders and pioneers of this movement, characterized by its glamour, energy, art school sensibilities, and a pervasive attitude of "doom and gloom" that became infectious and spread worldwide. "The group was one of the founders and pioneers of the original British Goth movement. The glamour, the energy, the art school sensibilities, and the attitude of doom and gloom proved to be infectious."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Bauhaus?

podcast.title: British Invention and Rapid Spread
podcast.body: Goth was a British invention that emerged rapidly in the wake of punk. Alongside other styles like Technopop, Industrial, and Modern Skah, it spread and often faded quickly due to the concentrated nature of the British Isles, which facilitated fast movement of ideas and trends. "There was Goth and Tecdopop and Industrial, Modern Skah, which were all basically British inventions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Invention with Early American Practitioners
podcast.body: Goth largely emerged in Britain in the late 1970s after punk rock declined, though early American artists like The Doors and The Velvet Underground had some sinister sounds. "goth is very much a British invention, with one tiny exception."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Origins
podcast.body: Goth music emerged as a significant byproduct of the British punk rock explosion of the 1970s, making it primarily a British creation, despite some early American involvement. "Goth music was one of the many different byproducts of the British end of the punk rock explosion of the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chocolate's Defining Sound
podcast.body: Gothic music was a core element of Chocolate's identity, which was known as "the darkest, the most gothic club on the Ruta." DJ Tony Vitale "El Gitano" specifically played "sinister" bands like Bauhaus, Cabaret Voltaire, and Throbbing Gristle, attracting clientele from the punk and sinister subcultures. "Fue el club más oscuro, el más gótico de todas las discotecas de la ruta."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Cuando Valencia fue la capital mundial del Clubbing

podcast.title: Cultural Context - Escapism in Early 80s
podcast.body: The theater, romance, horror, and angst of Goth provided an escape that went "far beyond the real life doom and gloom of the early 80s," a period marked by the Cold War and a global recession. Goth fans embraced the dark aesthetic, concluding that "since we're all going hell anyway, we might as well dress the part and dance towards the apocalypse." "The theater and romance and horror and angst of God went far beyond the real life doom and gloom of the early 80s, even with the Cold War and the global recession."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Bauhaus

podcast.title: Cultural Extension
podcast.body: The Goth culture extended beyond just music, encompassing clubs, magazines, and a general lifestyle, creating a comprehensive subculture for its practitioners and fans. "And the culture extended to clubs and magazines and a general lifestyle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: David Bowie's Endearment to Fans
podcast.body: David Bowie's portrayal of a vampire in the 1983 movie "The Hunger" endeared him to goth fans forever, solidifying his status as an influential figure within the subculture. His artistic exploration of darker themes and theatricality also resonated deeply with the goth aesthetic. "By the way, he played a vampire in The Hunger, something that endeared him to got fans forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discovery by Generation X
podcast.body: Generation X discovered various flavors of Goth music, which had existed outside the mainstream for years. "JNX discovered different flavors of Goth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Distinct Musical Sound
podcast.body: The Goth sound was identifiable by "fairly tribal" drums, bass players often playing high on the fretboard and carrying much of the melody, sharp and thin guitars, and singing that could be "almost operatic," often creating a hypnotic and mesmerizing effect. "For a while there was a Goth sound. The drums were fairly tribal. Bass players played high on the fretboard and sometimes carried much of the melody instead of just providing the rhythmic foundation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Meaning of "Gothic"
podcast.body: Initially, describing music as "Gothic" referred to its doomy, gloomy atmosphere, drawing parallels to themes found in 19th-century Gothic literature, such as Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," and even older Gothic architecture or the Visigoths. "At first, describing music as Gothic meant that it had a doomy gloomy atmosphere."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence in Post-Punk Era
podcast.body: Goth emerged in the "very late 1970s" during the post-punk era, a time when punk had emboldened people to experiment, leading to the development of dark sounds and sensibilities. "Goth emerged in the very late 1970s during a time when punk had emboldened people to try all kinds of different things."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence of Goth Music
podcast.body: Goth music did not widely emerge until bands like Bauhaus appeared in the late 1970s. This historical context is used to compare with the earlier visual and musical elements of "proto-goth" seen in the 1974 film "Phantom of the Paradise."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ethereal and Spooky Feel
podcast.body: Much of Goth music was characterized by an ethereal and spooky atmosphere, often dark, in minor keys, and sometimes infused with romantic notions and supernatural themes, creating an "otherworldly" sound.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Etymology of "Goths"
podcast.body: One story suggests British punk refugees who made gloomy music were called "goths" because they lived in an apartment building named Visigoth Towers in Brixton, London. Alternatively, music journalist Nick Kent may have coined the term. "One story says they became known as goths because a bunch of them all lived in the same apartment building, a place called Visigoth Towers in the Brixton area of London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution and Influence (Mid-80s)
podcast.body: By the mid-1980s, Goth's influence extended to other genres, including new industrial bands and electronic groups, and even some metal acts, demonstrating its pervasive and lasting impact. "By the mid-80s Goth's influence was spilling over into other genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fashion Aesthetics
podcast.body: Goth fashion, often called "menacing" or "disconcerting" to outsiders, is characterized by wearing all black, except for occasional shades of purple or bright red (especially lipstick). Styles often harken back to 19th-century British artsy class attire, some androgenous, others BDSM-inspired, creating an erotic, mysterious, "dressed for a never-ending funeral" look. "This insistence on wearing black everything became part of the glue that held the new scene together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fresh Approach in Early 1990s
podcast.body: Goth music saw a "fresh approach" in the early 1990s, indicating an evolution or revitalization of the genre during that period. "along with a fresh approach to Goth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Global Reach as Rock Subculture
podcast.body: Goth has the potential to be the largest rock-related subculture globally, influencing music, comic books, cartoons, fashion, television, and movies, to the extent that it's suggested director Tim Burton's work wouldn't exist without it. "Goth could very well be the biggest rock-related subculture in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Goth / Gothic Rock – Joy Division and The Cure into Bauhaus, Alien Sex Fiend, Siouxsie
podcast.body: Gothic rock began with dark, somber, bleak groups such as Joy Division and The Cure, then got darker with groups like Bauhaus, Alien Sex Fiend, and Siouxsie and the Banshees. The genre focused on the dark side of music, often with genuine Gothic overtones drawn from the original Gothic culture of the 1800s — elements of doom, sometimes romantic, occasionally supernatural. "Goth or Gothic Rock, which focused on the dark side of the music, often with genuine Gothic overtones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historical Roots
podcast.body: Goth is presented as a genre with deep historical roots, dating back to 1818, indicating a long lineage of influences that predates its musical emergence. The discussion of this genre is set to explore its birth and development. "And this genre was a long time coming, since 1818, in fact, we'll look at the birth of Goth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Identity Marker
podcast.body: Goth is cited as a music genre that comes with specific fashion trends, which individuals might adopt to utilize music as an "identity marker." This allows them to project their identity and form friendships within a community of shared musical and aesthetic preferences.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Influence from Joy Division
podcast.body: The sound and style of Joy Division are credited with contributing significantly to the development of Goth music. "Their sound and style contributed to everything from the development of Goth to industrial music to Emo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Influence of Glam Rock
podcast.body: Goth, gaining traction in 1979, was a direct descendant of glam, inheriting its theatricality and fashion-forward (or backward) sensibility. "No Glam, no Goth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Influences and Themes
podcast.body: Many early Goth bands were inspired by images and attitudes from Gothic novels and 1800s fashions, sometimes incorporating elements of the occult and the bizarre, with lyrics often described as "introspective" and "dark." "Many of them were inspired by images and attitudes from Gothic novels and fashions of the 1800s and earlier. Elements of the occult and the bizarre were sometimes incorporated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Initial Musical Characteristics
podcast.body: Early Goth music was less aggressive and more introspective and artsy than punk. It included an intellectual component, incorporating elements of traditional Gothic horror, existentialist philosophy, romanticism, and nihilism, alongside inspirations from monsters, The Addams Family, B-horror movies from the 1950s and 60s, and The Rocky Horror Picture Show. "Early Goth music was less aggressive than punk. It was also introspective and artsy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: King of Pain - Almost Goth
podcast.body: Sting's song "King of Pain" from "Synchronicity" was described as "super emo, almost goth," pointing to its dark, emotional aesthetic. "In the fall of 83, Sting's Super Emo, almost goth, King of Pain, reached number three on the Hot 100."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: If You Love Sting, Set Him Free Edition Part 1

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: If You Love Sting, Set Him Free Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Los Angeles Term
podcast.body: The term "death rock" was used in Los Angeles for a period to describe a specific aspect of the scene. "In Los Angeles, the word death rock was thrown around for a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Alt Rock Subgenre
podcast.body: Goth was identified as one of the biggest alt-rock subgenres and potentially "the second biggest rock genre in the world after metal," highlighting its extensive reach and popularity. "This is one of the biggest alt rock subgenres and might be the second biggest rock genre in the world after metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Meaning of "Gothic" in Music
podcast.body: The word "gothic" was first used to describe modern music in relation to The Doors' first album, due to its dark, mysterious, and violent qualities. "As far as we can tell, the first use of the word gothic to describe modern music was used in relation to the doors, first album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Misconceptions and Stigma
podcast.body: Despite common misconceptions, being Goth is not synonymous with being a psychopath. The subculture faces stigma due to the actions of a "tiny, tiny, tiny few" extremists who commit violent acts like the Columbine or Dawson College shootings. While Goth fashion and music can be dark, adherents are typically highly opinionated and not inherently evil. "To be Goth or to be Intugoth is not to be a psychopath."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Characteristics
podcast.body: Goth music featured "sharp, slashing guitars," bass lines often played higher up in the fretboard, and "heavy" drums, all working together to create a "hypnotic effect." "The music featured sharp, slashing guitars, bass lines that were often played higher up in the fretboard and drums that were heavy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Characteristics
podcast.body: Early Goth music featured tribal drums, bass players working high on the fretboard (sometimes carrying the melody), sharp, slashing, thin guitar sounds, and vocals ranging from growls to yelps to operatic. The overall effect was often described as mesmerizing. "In the beginning, there was almost a Goth sound, tribal drums, bass players working high on the fretboard, sometimes carrying the melody, which of course was just not done in proper circles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin as a Subculture
podcast.body: Goth music culture is one of the biggest musical subcultures globally, with its explosion beginning after the original punk era of the 1970s. It's speculated to be the second biggest music-related subculture after metal, encompassing music, fashion, art, lifestyle, and sometimes politics and religion. "goth music culture is one of the biggest musical subcultures the planet has ever seen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Peter Murphy's Status
podcast.body: Peter Murphy was described as a "Goth God" when Nine Inch Nails opened for him in 1990. "Nine H. Nails were opening for Goth God Peter Murphy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Punk Genesis
podcast.body: After the original punk scene fragmented, darker-minded punks gravitated towards artists already making dark music. This music, often less aggressive and more introspective and artsy than punk, incorporated existentialist philosophy, romanticism, art history, nihilism, and macabre horror elements. "As the original punk scene lost its legs, it began shattering into many different pieces. The darker-minded punk slowly coalesced around artists who were already making dark music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Punk Movement and Fashion (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: In the early 1980s, Goth emerged as a significant post-punk movement, characterized by a distinctive fashion style that was as dark as the mood of its music. Bands like The Cure became prominent figures within this scene, with their aesthetic and sound influencing millions globally. "In the early 1980s, one of the great post-punk movements was known as Gough, Dark Stuff, and the fashion was as black as the mood of the music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 6

podcast.title: Post-Punk Subgenre
podcast.body: Goth is identified as a major post-punk genre that emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and is one of the genres that "are still with us today." "There was new wave, techno pop, and all its subsets, industrial music, goth, and a revival of scot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Prominent 1980s Youth Culture
podcast.body: Goth was identified as one of the prominent youth cultures of the 1980s, alongside Blitzkids, Hip Hop, and the explosion of Acid House, each having its own distinct aesthetic and sound. "Tuvimos la cena God, los Blitzkits, El Hig Hop, la explosión de la Siddhaw..."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El oscuro origen de la música de los KEYGEN

podcast.title: Quiet Continued Growth
podcast.body: After the initial mainstream peak, Goth continued to grow and expand, but in a more "quiet" manner. "So what happened next? Well, Goth got bigger. But quietly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reclaiming the Term "Goth"
podcast.body: Initially an insult, the term "Goth" was reclaimed by the scene by the summer of 1982, becoming a self-identifier. "At the beginning, to be called Goth was an insult. But by the summer of 1982, the scene reclaimed that word as their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reclamation of "Goth" Term
podcast.body: Initially, "Goth" was used as an insult, but by the summer of 1982, the nascent scene reclaimed the word as its official name, demonstrating self-identification and community. "Now, at first, to be called a Goth was an insult. But by the summer of 1982, the scene reclaimed that word as its name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Resilience and Longevity
podcast.body: Goth has proven to be one of the most resilient and long-lasting alternative rock subgenres to emerge from the post-punk era, consistently remaining in the cultural background and influencing new generations of bands with a darker perspective on life. "Goth has proven to be one of the most resilient and long-lasting of the alt-rock subgenres that emerged from the post-punk era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Roots in Punk Refugee Movement
podcast.body: A considerable number of punk refugees gravitated towards dark, gloomy music during a period of high unemployment, strikes, and recession in England, which was particularly difficult for young people. This collective turn towards darkness helped form the Goth scene. "Whatever the case, a significant number of punk refugees began to turn towards dark gloomy music because it was... Well, it was a dark gloomy time in England."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Strength and Conviction over Whining
podcast.body: Despite its dark and introspective nature, Goth was characterized as possessing strength and conviction rather than being "whiny," a quality that was celebrated. "Now, despite this darkness, Goth was never whiny. Introspective, maybe, but there was a strength there, a strength and a conviction that needed to be celebrated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Subculture Characteristics
podcast.body: Goth is a comprehensive subculture that carefully controls its membership, encompassing music, art, fashion, lifestyle, and sometimes religion and politics, with varying levels of adherence from casual dabblers to devoted hardcore members. "Goth is a subculture. And it really is a full blown subculture. It carefully guards its membership."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Subgenre of Post-Punk
podcast.body: Goth is identified as one of the styles that falls under the post-punk umbrella. "Goth, dark wave, dream pop, the jangly guitars, bands like R.E.M., the spiky stuff of groups like Wire and Shoegay's were, and in some cases still are, artists in those buckets that we can consider to be post-punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Theater of Hate as an Example
podcast.body: The band Theater of Hate is cited as an example of a goth band. "Steve Guthrie was a member of a Gothband called Theater of Hate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK Origin
podcast.body: A significant portion of this early Goth music originated from the UK.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
